notes: Kingship or reign: God's rule, not mainly a territory. Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven" where Mark and Luke say "kingdom of God," likely a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. It's the theme of Jesus' preaching from his first words (4:17).

range.note: The right and power to rule.
The people or territory a king rules.
The age when God's will is done on earth as in heaven.

elsewhere.note: "The kingdom of God has come near."
"The kingdom of God is among you."
Righteousness, peace, and joy.
"The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord."

notes: Doing what is right before God and toward others. In Matthew it's mostly about how people actually live (5:20, 6:1), with a sense of being in the right with God. Paul later uses the same word for the right standing God gives.

range.note: Living in line with God's will.
Fairness and rightness in dealings with others.
Being declared in the right before God (especially in Paul).

elsewhere.note: God's righteousness revealed in the gospel.
Righteousness through faith.
"That we might become the righteousness of God."
Abraham counted righteous.

notes: To fill up or complete. Matthew uses it again and again for Scripture reaching its full meaning in Jesus ("this was to fulfill"). Sometimes that's a prediction coming true; sometimes it's a pattern in Israel's story repeated in his, as with "Out of Egypt I called my son" (2:15).

range.note: Make something full, like a net (13:48).
Finish or bring to an end.
Show what a Scripture was pointing toward.

elsewhere.note: "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled."
Fulfilling what is written in the law.
Love fulfills the law.
The whole law fulfilled in one command.

notes: Literally "to change one's mind," but in the Bible it means turning around: a change of heart and direction toward God. Behind it stands the Hebrew prophets' call to "turn" (shuv). It's the first word of both John's and Jesus' preaching in Matthew.

range.note: Think again about something.
Regret and leave behind what was wrong.
A new direction for the whole life.

elsewhere.note: "Repent and believe the good news."
Joy in heaven over one who repents.
Peter's call at Pentecost.
A call to a church to return.

notes: Originally a priestly class among the Medes and Persians. By the first century the word covered experts in stars, dreams, and hidden knowledge, and could also mean a sorcerer. Matthew doesn't say how many came or that they were kings; those ideas came later.
uncertain: Who exactly the visitors were, and whether they came from Persia, Babylon, or Arabia, is debated.

range.note: A member of the Magian class.
Someone who interprets signs in the sky.
A negative sense, as in Acts 13.

elsewhere.note: Bar-Jesus, a magician on Cyprus.
Elymas "the magician."

notes: The Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Immanu-el. Matthew translates it for his readers, and the book ends on the same note: "I am with you always" (28:20).

range.note: Given in Isaiah's sign to King Ahaz.

elsewhere.note: The sign of the child (in Hebrew).

notes: Greek for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one" (Messiah). Kings and priests were anointed with oil; by Jesus' time many hoped for an anointed king from David's line who would set Israel free. In Matthew it's still a title, not yet a surname.

range.note: Marked out with oil for a role.
The promised king from David's line.
Later, almost a second name ("Jesus Christ").

"We have found the Messiah."
"Both Lord and Christ."
Declared Son of God in power.

notes: Describes someone in a good place, especially as God sees it. It's a declaration, not an instruction: Jesus isn't telling people to mourn, but saying that those who mourn are in God's favor. Some translations try "happy," which can sound too light.

range.note: Well off, to be congratulated.
In God's favor, whatever things look like now.
In ordinary Greek, simply happy or prosperous.

Blessed is the one who endures trials.

notes: In Greek theater the word meant an actor, someone playing a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for people whose devotion is a performance for an audience. Matthew uses it more than any other book.

notes: An Aramaic word for wealth or property, carried over into Greek. Jesus pictures it as a rival master that competes with God for loyalty, which is why older translations kept it as a name, "Mammon."
